876.title: Umar's death
876.hook: stabbed at dawn prayer, he names a council of six to choose his successor
876.howItsDone: Muslims retell Umar's death from the long report in Sahih al-Bukhari, and the council he named is taught in Sunni history as the shura that chose Uthman; his grave lies beside the Prophet's and Abu Bakr's in Medina.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the plague, and a caravan that turned back. Your line was don't enter, don't leave.

Dawn in the mosque at Medina. The rows are forming. Umar walks between them as he used to before the prayer, telling people to straighten their lines. He takes his place at the front and says God is greatest. And in that moment a man steps out of the dark and stabs him. A man named Amr ibn Maymun was standing in the rows, and Bukhari keeps what he saw. Today: Umar's death.
screen: `DAWN, AND THE ROWS FORMING.` → `GOD IS GREATEST.` → `A MAN STEPS OUT OF THE DARK.`

segments.voice: Umar falls, and the first thing he does is reach for Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf's hand and pull him forward to lead the prayer. The prayer goes on, short and quiet. Afterward Umar asks who struck him. A slave of al-Mughirah, he's told. And Umar says: praise be to God, who did not let my death come at the hands of a man who claims Islam. They bring him milk to drink, and it comes out of the wound, and the people around him understand. A young man comes in and praises him: your companionship with the Prophet, your justice. Umar answers: I wish it would come out even, nothing against me and nothing for me. Then he sends his son Abdullah to Aisha with a request: may Umar be buried beside his two companions? She says she had wanted the place for herself, but she will give it to him. Then the question everyone is waiting for: who leads next? Umar does not name a son. He does not name one man. He names six, the companions with whom, he says, the Prophet was pleased when he died: Ali, Uthman, al-Zubayr, Talhah, Sa'd and Abd al-Rahman. Let them choose one from among themselves. His own son may sit with them, but have no share in the choice. The Qur'an praises those whose affairs are settled by consultation among them, and Umar made his last act a consultation. Sunni Muslims honor this council as the way Uthman was chosen; Shia Muslims, as with the succession, read these events differently. The council itself is tomorrow's story.
screen: `HE PULLS ABD AL-RAHMAN FORWARD.` · `NOT BY ONE WHO CLAIMS ISLAM.` · `BURIED BESIDE HIS TWO COMPANIONS.` · `SIX NAMED. NO SON, NO HEIR.` · then, large: `A COUNCIL, NOT A CROWN.`

segments.voice: Picture the mosque before sunrise, the rows straight, the quiet, and a man who, wounded, made sure the prayer went on. If you pray, you might pray fajr tomorrow, at the hour Umar stood in the rows; if you don't, you might wake a little early and sit for a minute at first light.
Umar's death. Stabbed as he began the dawn prayer, he had the prayer go on, asked to be buried beside his two companions, and named six to choose from among themselves. Today's word.
Your line: a council, not a crown. No son, no heir: six to choose. Day eight hundred seventy-six, done.

877.title: Uthman's caliphate
877.hook: the gentle Uthman rules as lands and a navy grow
877.howItsDone: Sunni Muslims honor Uthman as the third rightly guided caliph and remember his modesty and generosity; Shia Muslims hold that Ali was the rightful leader, and Shia tellings dwell on the complaints against Uthman's rule.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Umar's death. Struck at the dawn prayer, he left the choice to a council of six. Your line was a council, not a crown.

Should I not feel shy before a man the angels feel shy before? Sahih Muslim reports the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, asking that about one of his companions. The scene is small. The Prophet is resting at home, his clothes loosely arranged. Abu Bakr comes in, and he stays as he is. Umar comes in, and he stays as he is. Then Uthman asks to enter, and the Prophet sits up and straightens his garment. Aisha asks him why. His answer is that question. After Umar's death, the council chose this man: Uthman ibn Affan.
screen: `THE PROPHET SITS UP.` → `THE ANGELS FEEL SHY.` → `THE COUNCIL CHOOSES UTHMAN.`

segments.voice: Bukhari records how. The men Umar named narrowed it among themselves, and Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, giving up his own claim, was trusted to choose between Ali and Uthman. He spent nights consulting people, the report says, then took Uthman's hand and pledged to him, and the people followed. Uthman came with a reputation. In Bukhari's reports he answered the Prophet's call to provide the well of Rumah for the people, and to equip the army in a time of hardship. Wealthy, quiet, generous, modest. Under his rule the lands of the Muslims kept growing, and something new happened: ships. Bukhari tells of Umm Haram, who heard the Prophet describe people of his community riding the sea like kings on thrones, and asked him to pray she would be one of them. The report says she later sailed, in the days of Mu'awiyah, Uthman's governor of Syria, and the histories set that voyage in Uthman's time. Now the harder part. Gentleness in a ruler reads two ways. His admirers see mercy: a caliph slow to punish, open-handed with his own money. His critics, in his own lifetime, said he gave too many posts to relatives and was too slow to remove governors people complained about. The sources record both. Sunni Muslims honor him as the third rightly guided caliph and one of the companions promised paradise. Shia Muslims hold that Ali should have led from the start, and Shia tellings dwell on the complaints. Both readings sit side by side here, because the complaints will grow.
screen: `ABD AL-RAHMAN CONSULTS FOR NIGHTS.` · `A WELL PROVIDED, AN ARMY EQUIPPED.` · `UMM HARAM AND THE SEA.` · `MERCY, OR TOO SOFT?` · then, large: `GENTLE RULE.`

segments.voice: Pick one small kingdom where others depend on your decisions: a kitchen, a classroom, a shift you run, even a dog. Remember a moment there when you were sharper than you needed to be, and replay it with the same firmness and a softer voice. If you pray, you can ask for mercy in how you lead.
Uthman's caliphate: a modest, generous man chosen by the council after Umar, a time of growth and ships at sea, and complaints that would not go away. Today's word.
Your line: gentle rule. Firm and gentle can live in the same voice. See you tomorrow.

878.title: One reading for all
878.hook: Uthman sends standard copies of the Qur'an to the cities to unite the reading
878.howItsDone: Muslims call a written copy of the Qur'an a mushaf and commonly keep it in a clean, raised place; printed copies today follow the written text remembered as Uthman's, and recognized recitations are still taught.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Uthman's caliphate. A modest man, a growing realm, ships at sea, and complaints beginning. Your line was gentle rule.

A soldier comes home from the far frontier, and what troubles him is not the enemy. It's his own side. The man is Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, and Bukhari tells what he saw on campaign in the north. Muslims from Syria and Muslims from Iraq were serving together, and when they recited the Qur'an, they recited it differently, and they argued about it. Hudhayfah rides to Medina and goes straight to Uthman. Commander of the faithful, he says, in effect, save this community before it divides over its own book.
screen: `A SOLDIER COMES HOME WORRIED.` → `TWO ARMIES, TWO READINGS.` → `SAVE THE COMMUNITY.`

segments.voice: Bukhari's report is short and practical. Uthman sends to Hafsah, the Prophet's widow and Umar's daughter, who keeps the sheets of the Qur'an gathered in Abu Bakr's time, and borrows them. He gives the work to Zayd ibn Thabit, who had written revelation for the Prophet, with men of Quraysh, and tells them: where you differ with Zayd over how a word is written, write it in the speech of Quraysh, because the Qur'an came down in their tongue. They copy the sheets into books. The sheets go back to Hafsah. A copy goes out to each province, with an order that other written collections be burned. That may startle a modern listener. The tradition reads it as the opposite of disrespect: one agreed text, so no one would fight over private copies with their own additions and gaps. Reports say Ali, asked about it later, defended what Uthman did with the copies. Muslims call a written copy a mushaf, and the standard copies are remembered as Uthman's. The Qur'an speaks of who keeps it. In Pickthall's translation: "Lo! We, even We, reveal the Reminder, and lo! We verily are its Guardian." Tradition reads Uthman's work as one way that promise was carried out by human hands. And the different ways of reciting were not erased: recognized recitations, the qira'at, are still learned and recited. Unity of the written text, not one single voice.

segments.voice: Look at where your Qur'an sits, on a high shelf or under a coffee cup; if you don't have one, choose any book that matters to you, a scripture, a family Bible, a grandparent's letters. Notice its weight, its wear, the hands it has passed through. If you can, move it somewhere cleaner and higher, or simply wipe the cover.
Mushaf, a written copy of the Qur'an: Uthman's standard copies, made from Hafsah's sheets and sent to the provinces, so the community would share one written text. Today's word.
Your line: one text for all. A shared page can settle what memory can't. Day eight hundred seventy-eight, done.

879.title: The siege
879.hook: grievances grow, rebels surround his house, and he refuses to let blood be shed for him
879.howItsDone: The histories name the siege of Uthman as the start of the fitnah; Sunni teachers cite his refusal to let Muslims fight on his behalf, and Shia tellings put the weight on the grievances behind the revolt.

segments.voice: Yesterday: mushaf. Hafsah's sheets became Zayd's copies, one for each province. Your line was one text for all.

The street outside the caliph's house is full of armed men, and they are not foreign soldiers. They are Muslims, from Egypt and the garrison towns of Iraq, with complaints about governors, appointments and money. They have camped in Medina, and they want Uthman to step down. He will not take off what God has put on him, he says. So they close in on his house. Inside are a few companions and young men, among them, the histories say, Hasan, the Prophet's grandson, sent by Ali to guard the door. They have swords. And the old man inside tells them to put the swords away.
screen: `ARMED MEN IN THE STREET.` → `STEP DOWN, THEY SAY.` → `PUT THE SWORDS AWAY.`

segments.voice: Fitnah. In the Qur'an the word carries trial, temptation and testing, and the lexicons connect the root with smelting gold in fire to see what is real. Later Muslims also use it for civil strife, Muslim against Muslim, a test of a different kind. The histories give the name to the years that begin at Uthman's door. Why did he refuse a defense? The sources point back to the Prophet. Bukhari records a day when the Prophet sat at a well and the companions came one by one asking to enter. For Abu Bakr: give him the good news of paradise. For Umar, the same. For Uthman: the good news of paradise, with a trial that will befall him. Uthman answered, the report says: God is the one whose help is sought. And Tirmidhi records the Prophet telling Uthman that God might clothe him in a shirt, and if people wanted him to take it off, he should not. Uthman read these as a calling: keep the office, and don't let Muslims kill Muslims to save his life. So, the histories report, he told those guarding him to go home, and told the servants who would fight that whoever laid down his weapon was free. Readers have argued ever since. Holiness, or handing the city to the rebels? Sunni tradition honors it as the restraint of a martyr. Shia tellings put the weight on the grievances he had not answered. The sources agree on the core: he forbade fighting for him.
screen: `FITNAH: TRIAL BY FIRE.` · `PARADISE, WITH A TRIAL.` · `DO NOT TAKE OFF THE SHIRT.` · `GO HOME. LAY DOWN YOUR WEAPON.` · then, large: `HE FORBADE FIGHTING FOR HIM.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one live conflict: a family thread, a neighbor, a coworker, a comment section. Find the move you've been tempted to make, the reply that would bring in your allies, and set it down, without giving up what's right. If you pray, you can ask for help in the trial.
Fitnah. Trial and testing in the Qur'an, and later the name for strife among Muslims, beginning, the histories say, with the siege of Uthman's house. Today's word.
Your line: he forbade fighting for him. Restraint can be its own kind of courage. That's day eight hundred seventy-nine.

880.title: Uthman killed
880.hook: Uthman is killed in his house, reading the Qur'an
880.howItsDone: Sunni Muslims remember Uthman as a martyr killed while reading the Qur'an and often pray for mercy on him when his name is mentioned; Shia Muslims remember the event as part of the history that led to Ali's caliphate.

segments.voice: Yesterday: fitnah, a trial that tests what is real. Uthman sent his defenders home. Your line was he forbade fighting for him.

On the mountain of Uhud, years earlier, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, stood with three companions: Abu Bakr, Umar and Uthman. Bukhari reports that the mountain trembled, and the Prophet said to it: be still, Uhud, for on you are a prophet, a man of truth, and two martyrs. Umar had already died that way, struck at prayer. Now the second martyr in that saying comes due. Uthman's friends have put their swords away, as he asked. The swords outside have not.
screen: `THE MOUNTAIN TREMBLES.` → `A PROPHET, A MAN OF TRUTH, TWO MARTYRS.` → `THE SECOND MARTYR COMES DUE.`

segments.voice: The histories tell it plainly, with some differences in detail. The defenders have gone home. Uthman is in his room with a copy of the Qur'an open in front of him, reading. Some reports say he was fasting that day, and had seen the Prophet in a dream the night before, telling him he would break his fast with him. The attackers come in, some say over the wall from a neighboring house. His wife, Na'ilah, throws herself between him and the blade, and her hand is cut. Uthman is struck while the book is still open. Tradition says his blood fell on a verse of the second surah, a line in which God promises to be enough against those who oppose. Whether or not every detail is exact, the picture the tradition keeps is your line: an old man, unarmed, killed with the book open. For Sunni Muslims he is a martyr, the man the angels feel shy before, a companion promised paradise. Shia Muslims, who hold that leadership belonged to Ali, don't honor his rule in the same way, and their historians emphasize the grievances that came before. Across those differences, the histories tell it as a catastrophe: a caliph of the Muslims killed by Muslims in the city of the Prophet. The fitnah was no longer a threat. It had arrived, and the question of who would lead next would split the community for years to come.

881.title: Ali, caliph
881.hook: Ali accepts the caliphate in a divided city, the fourth caliph for Sunnis, the first Imam for Shia
881.howItsDone: Sunni Muslims honor Ali as the fourth rightly guided caliph; Shia Muslims honor him as the first Imam, appointed by the Prophet, and both remember the hadith of Aaron and Moses about him.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Uthman killed, in his own house, unarmed. Your line was killed with the book open.

Who wants a crown the day after the last man wearing it was murdered? Medina is in shock. The rebels are still in the streets, and the city needs someone to lead it, today. The people go to one man's door: Ali ibn Abi Talib, the Prophet's cousin, raised in his house, married to his daughter Fatimah. And the reports say his first answer was no. Leave me, he tells them, find someone else; I would rather be your helper than your ruler. They keep coming back.
screen: `A CITY IN SHOCK.` → `THEY GO TO ALI'S DOOR.` → `LEAVE ME, HE SAYS.`

segments.voice: In the end, the histories say, Ali agreed, on one condition: the pledge would be made openly, in the mosque, where everyone could see. So he became caliph in a divided city, and some companions held back from pledging at all. Here Muslims tell the same story two ways, and both deserve to be heard plainly. For Sunni Muslims, Ali is the fourth of the rightly guided caliphs, after Abu Bakr, Umar and Uthman, each chosen in turn, all four honored. For Shia Muslims, Ali is the first Imam, the one the Prophet named to lead after him, and the three before him held an office that was rightfully his. Same man, same day, two counts. Both traditions keep one saying about him. In Bukhari's telling, when the Prophet left Ali behind in Medina during a campaign, Ali was unhappy, and the Prophet said: are you not content to be to me as Aaron was to Moses, except that there will be no prophet after me? Shia collections carry it too. And the saying from Ghadir Khumm, met earlier, returns with new weight: of whomever I am the mawla, Ali is his mawla. A word of love and loyalty, in the Sunni reading; an appointment to lead, in the Shia reading. Either way, the man who took up the office that day was not taking a prize. He was taking on a fitnah already burning, and a community that would not agree on how to count him.

882.title: The Battle of the Camel
882.hook: Aisha, Talhah and Zubayr oppose Ali, and believers fight believers
882.howItsDone: Sunni Muslims teach the Battle of the Camel as a tragedy among honored companions who acted on their judgment; Shia Muslims teach it as Ali's rightful defense of his caliphate. Both recite the verse on making peace between two parties of believers.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ali, pledged openly in the mosque and counted two ways. Your line was the fourth; the first.

A camel stands in the middle of a battlefield outside Basra. On its back is a covered litter, and inside is Aisha, the Prophet's widow, the woman Muslims call a mother of the believers. Around the camel, men are dying to protect it. Facing them is the army of Ali, the Prophet's cousin. With Aisha are Talhah and Zubayr, two companions the Prophet had promised paradise. Every name on this field belongs to the Prophet's own circle. That is what makes the day so hard to tell.
screen: `A CAMEL ON THE FIELD.` → `AISHA IN THE LITTER.` → `THE PROPHET'S OWN CIRCLE.`

segments.voice: How did it come to this? Uthman's killers were still among the crowds. Aisha, Talhah and Zubayr demanded that justice for his blood come first. Ali held that the state had to be steadied before the guilty could be found and punished. Both sides wanted justice for Uthman; they disagreed about the order. Aisha's party went to Basra, and Ali followed. The histories say talks went far and a settlement seemed close, and then fighting broke out, some reports say in the night, stirred up by men who feared any peace would expose them. Bukhari keeps a moment from just before. Ammar ibn Yasir, on Ali's side, stands in the pulpit at Kufa and says of Aisha: she is the wife of your Prophet in this world and the next, but God is testing you, whether you will obey Him or her. Even from the other side, Ammar would not speak of her without honor. The Qur'an had already named this kind of day. In Pickthall's translation: "And if two parties of believers fall to fighting, then make peace between them." The verse does not say one side stops being believers. Ali's army won. Talhah and Zubayr were killed. The histories say Ali sent Aisha back to Medina with honor and an escort. Sunni teaching holds that the companions on both sides acted on their best judgment, and honors them all. Shia Muslims hold that Ali was in the right and that those who fought him erred. Your line holds what both sides grieve.
